data: NASA Discovery polar orbiter — neutron-spectrometer hydrogen finding at both poles 1998; deliberate Shoemaker impact ended mission 1999

The third NASA Discovery-class mission and the first dedicated US lunar mission since Explorer 49 (1973). Launched 1998-01-07 on an Athena II from Cape Canaveral, Lunar Prospector was captured into lunar orbit on 1998-01-11 and lowered to a 100-km polar mapping orbit on 16 January. Its neutron spectrometer detected sharp neutron-flux deficits over both lunar poles (Feldman et al., 1998 / 1999) — consistent with 10–300 million tonnes of water ice (1998 estimate) in permanently shadowed polar craters. The gravimeter, magnetometer, gamma-ray and alpha-particle spectrometers also delivered global maps of crustal composition and remnant magnetism. End of mission 1999-07-31: deliberately impacted in Shoemaker crater hoping to release a detectable water-vapour plume; none was seen (the lithium-7 fluorescence experiment that would have detected it was a long shot). The hydrogen finding stood until LCROSS (2009) and Chandrayaan-1 / M3 (2009) provided independent confirmation.
Feldman et al. (1998) — Fluxes of fast and epithermal neutrons from Lunar Prospector (Science 281)

The third NASA Discovery-class mission (and the first competitively selected) and the first dedicated NASA science mission to the Moon since Explorer 49 (1973). Launched 1998-01-07 on an Athena II from Cape Canaveral, Lunar Prospector was captured into lunar orbit on 1998-01-11 and lowered to a 100-km polar mapping orbit on 16 January. Its neutron spectrometer detected sharp neutron-flux deficits over both lunar poles (Feldman et al., 1998 / 1999) — consistent with 10–300 million tonnes of water ice (1998 estimate) in permanently shadowed polar craters. The gravimeter, magnetometer, gamma-ray and alpha-particle spectrometers also delivered global maps of crustal composition and remnant magnetism. End of mission 1999-07-31: deliberately impacted in Shoemaker crater hoping to release a detectable water-vapour plume; none was seen (the lithium-7 fluorescence experiment that would have detected it was a long shot). The hydrogen finding stood until LCROSS (2009) and Chandrayaan-1 / M3 (2009) provided independent confirmation.
Neutron-spectrometer hydrogen finding at both lunar poles
Longest-lived Mars asset ever — orbiting since 2001-10-24. Gamma-ray + neutron water-ice maps; UHF relay for the surface fleet
First Mercury orbiter — 6 planetary gravity assists over 6.6 years to bleed energy before insertion in 2011
Only spacecraft to orbit two extraterrestrial worlds — Vesta then Ceres via ion propulsion
First Jupiter orbiter; 8 years of measurements

Direct neutron-spectrometer detection of hydrogen at both lunar poles — strong evidence for water ice in permanently-shadowed crater floors. Deliberately impacted into Shoemaker crater at end of mission, hoping the impact ejecta would confirm water; Earth-based observers detected nothing definitive (a follow-up only delivered by LCROSS in 2009).
